summary: A request for comments on using the ARPANET's resources for Computer Based Instruction. It describes existing standalone and centralized systems and asks the community how network resources might be applied, aiming to start a dialogue.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 313 considers how a general computer network could support computer-based instruction. It describes several possible uses and asks educators and network researchers to discuss them.

questions: how could a network support computer based instruction
what network resources could help develop courses
subtitle: How a general computer network might support instruction

tldr.problem: The author says the potential use of general-purpose networks for computer-based instruction was not widely understood.
tldr.mechanism: The paper discusses network access, centralized storage, language processors and online tools for discussion as possible support for instruction.
tldr.outcome: It invites comments and starts a discussion rather than specifying a particular instructional system.

today: RFC 313 is a discussion paper about possible uses of general-purpose network resources for computer-based instruction. It asks readers to comment on the opportunities and implementation questions.

sections.title: Instruction Has Several Computing Needs
sections.content:
The paper describes computer-based instruction as including course design, field testing, distribution and operation, and later evaluation and revision. Its computing needs depend on the teaching strategy and can include data, specialized processing and terminals at more than one location.

It distinguishes computer-aided instruction, where a computer presents lessons or tests, from computer-managed instruction, where a computer helps guide or organize teaching.
sections.plainLanguage: Computer-based instruction can present lessons or help manage them. Different teaching plans need different computers, data and ways for students to connect.

sections.title: Four Possible Network Contributions
sections.content:
The author identifies four areas where a general-purpose network could help: connecting terminals to instructional systems, sharing centralized data storage, providing access to language processors on different computers, and supporting dialogue among researchers, developers and users.

Network access could also let a geographically isolated center try a remote system before deciding whether to install its own equipment.
sections.plainLanguage: A network could connect students to distant computers, share lesson data, provide different kinds of software, and help educators discuss their work.

sections.title: Tools for Development and Evaluation
sections.content:
The paper notes that instructional systems may need text handling, branching based on student answers, arithmetic exercises, simulations and statistical analysis. Different network computers could provide different parts of this work. The author also discusses using network resources to test courses, support geographically distributed trials and share student or course information.

The conclusion calls for both instructional developers and network specialists to consider these uses and the technical problems they raise.
sections.plainLanguage: Teaching programs need many kinds of software and analysis. The author suggests that networked computers could share these tasks and asks both communities to explore the idea.
